Chapter 35

The URL is the state

SvelteURLSearchParams, one debounced shallow goto, and the two markers that a single field could not be.

By the end of this chapter

Put the query, the range and the view in the address bar without a navigation per keystroke.

The argument is not tidiness. People find something in an observability tool and paste it into a chat, and state that lives in a component turns that link into an empty page — which is the entire product failing at the only moment it mattered.

The address bar also gives three things for free, each of which is real work otherwise: the back button undoes a change to the query, a reload does not lose it, and the server can render the first result rather than shipping an empty shell that fetches after hydration.

Why not goto on every keystroke

Because it is a navigation: a hundred history entries for a sentence, and a re-run of every load on the route. The shape that works is to edit a local reactive params object and sync it to the address bar when the edits settle — which is exactly what SvelteURLSearchParams is for.

A plain URLSearchParams in $state would need replacing wholesale on every edit to be reactive at all, and .set() on it would silently do nothing. This is the case the reactive built-ins exist for, and the mirror image of the virtualizer’s plain Map in chapter 28.

One marker cannot answer two questions

The first version had a single #synced field. It was wrong in a way no unit test would have found, and the end-to-end suite found it in one test.

Two fields: what the address bar last *said*, and what we last *wrote*. And the params are read inside untrack, so the adopt effect depends only on the URL — without which every keystroke re-runs it and the two would be conflated again by a different route.

Why a unit test would not have found it

Because both halves work in isolation. Typing updates the params; flushing writes them. The bug lives in the *interaction* between an effect that reads and an effect that writes, which only exists once both are mounted in a real page — and only shows up if you press Run inside the debounce window.

And a consequence worth naming

Arriving on ?q=from+logs with no range rewrites the URL to include it, once, shortly after load. That is deliberate: the address bar is the state, so it should say all of it — and a link copied a moment later then carries the whole view rather than the half somebody happened to type.

The write itself: a shallow goto

SvelteKit 3 folded pushState and replaceState into goto. shallow: true means "change the URL and page.state, run no load", and replace: true is the difference between one history entry per pause in typing and one per page. The old pair still exists, deprecated; the new spelling is better because *every* change to the address bar now goes through one function with one set of options — and because goto only accepts a URL that resolves to a route, which is where the next block comes in. (The early return in the middle has a section of its own, below.)

The class does not know its own route. The page hands it a function that turns a search string into a URL through resolve() from $app/paths, and the return type — ResolvedPathname — is the proof that the URL points at a route this app has. That is what keeps the goto typed, and what lets the class be tested with no router at all.

A write that is still settling belongs to one entry

A debounced write is a promise made to the address bar 400ms ahead of time, and the entry it was made to is not always the one that is current when it comes due. The end-to-end suite found that out under load, in a test that had passed every time before.

Two conditions on one effect. ownsAddressBar holds the write while the drawer’s trace URL is in the address bar, and lets the effect run again when the drawer closes, so the write is made after all, to the entry it was meant for. navigating.type !== null holds it while the router is in the middle of anything: a link, the back button, the drawer opening. Reading navigating is also what makes the effect run at the two moments that matter. When a navigation starts, the effect runs and its cleanup drops the waiting timer before the timer can take the navigation over. When the router is idle again, it runs once more and schedules whatever is still unwritten.

Where that second run lands depends on where the person went. A navigation to another page unmounts this one, effect and all, so nothing is written anywhere. A navigation back to this page, such as the header’s own Explore link, keeps the page mounted, and the edit goes to the entry the link made. A rule that only dropped the waiting write would get the first case right and the second wrong: the address bar would stay bare for good while the page showed a zoomed range.

The last word is the early return in #write, in the block above. It is for the one write that does not come through the effect: flush(), when somebody presses Run while the next page loads. It refuses during every navigation, shallow ones included. A shallow goto takes over a shallow navigation just as it takes over a real one, and refusing costs nothing, because the effect writes once the router is idle.

navigating.shallow type-checks, and it is undefined every time. navigating is declared as Navigation or an object of nulls, so once type !== null has narrowed it, TypeScript offers everything a Navigation has, shallow included. The object itself has getters for from, to, type, willUnload, delta and complete, the same list the documentation gives. shallow belongs to the objects handed to beforeNavigate, onNavigate and afterNavigate. A first draft of this guard tried to let shallow navigations through with !navigating.shallow, and in fact refused during all of them. That is now the rule on purpose.

Why the old replaceState did not race like this

The deprecated function is still in SvelteKit 3, and for backwards compatibility it runs no navigation hooks and leaves the router’s in-flight navigation alone. goto(url, { shallow: true }) is a navigation: it fires beforeNavigate, onNavigate and afterNavigate — the root layout’s view-transition guard depends on that — and it takes over whatever navigation the router is in the middle of. Going back to replaceState would only have changed the symptom. It would still have written the explore URL onto whichever entry was current: the drawer’s, or the trace page’s the moment the router had pushed it.

The in-effect changed for the same reason. In SvelteKit 3 page.url keeps describing the page as it was *rendered*; the address bar after a shallow goto is page.shallow.url. Adopting page.url was harmless while writes could not be held back. Once they can, it would undo a zoom made just before a trace was opened: closing the drawer goes back to an entry that SvelteKit renders from the page’s first URL.

A test that holds the window open

A race found under load is not proved fixed by a suite that passes under no load. These tests install Playwright’s clock and stop it once the page has written its URL out — which is also the proof that it hydrated, because only the client adds view — so "a write is waiting" is a fact the test arranged rather than a coincidence it hopes for. Each one checks that less than 400ms of page time has passed before the moment that matters, holds the next page’s request so its navigation is still in flight, then moves the clock past the debounce.

There are four, two for each half of the claim. Two check that nothing is written where it must not be: onto the drawer’s entry, or into a navigation to another page, and that includes pressing Run, which skips the effect and leaves only the guard in #write. The other two check that what was held back is still written: when the drawer closes, and when the navigation comes back to this page. Each was run against the code without the rule it covers, and failed at the step it targets.

A stopped clock stops more than your own timers. In async mode Svelte’s tick() resolves on a frame or a zero-length timeout, and on a clock that never moves neither comes — so the drawer waited for its data and then never painted, and the first version of these tests failed against the fixed code too. openTheDrawer moves the clock a millisecond at a time instead, which lets the frames through and stays nowhere near the 400ms.

Checkpoint

  • Typing a query updates the address bar once, not once per character.
  • The back button restores the previous query.
  • Pressing Run immediately after typing produces a correct URL.
  • Opening a trace within 400ms of an edit leaves the drawer open, and "Open full page" lands on the trace’s own URL.
  • Closing the drawer writes the edit that was waiting.
  • Pressing the header’s Explore link within 400ms of an edit still ends with the edit in the address bar.
